title: Relative Clauses: Places and Things That…

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know relative clauses with *que* and *quien* from B1 Unit 5: *que* joins a description to a noun (*la amiga que vive al lado*), and *quien* is for people, often after a preposition (*el vecino con quien hablamos*). The Dominican landscape is easy to describe this way: each mountain, bay or lake gets a clause that says where it is or what it does.

sections.title: One noun, one clause
rows: La bahía de Samaná, que está en el noreste, recibe ballenas.
*que* after a place: Samaná Bay, which is in the north-east
Las ballenas que llegan en enero vienen del Atlántico norte.
*que* with no commas says which whales: the whales that arrive in January
El guía con quien hablamos conoce el parque.
*quien* after a preposition, for a person: the guide we spoke with

items.spanish: El Pico Duarte, que mide más de tres mil metros, es la montaña más alta del Caribe.
items.english: Pico Duarte, which is over three thousand metres high, is the highest mountain in the Caribbean.

items.spanish: Los Haitises es un parque que protege manglares y colinas de roca caliza.
items.english: Los Haitises is a park that protects mangroves and limestone hills.

items.spanish: El lago Enriquillo, que es de agua salada, está bajo el nivel del mar.
items.english: Lake Enriquillo, which is a salt lake, is below sea level.

items.spanish: La guía con quien visitamos las cuevas conoce muy bien la historia de los taínos.
items.english: The guide we visited the caves with knows the history of the Taíno people very well.

sections.content: With commas, the clause adds extra information (*El lago Enriquillo, que es de agua salada, …*). Without commas, it says which one you mean (*las ballenas que llegan en enero*). *Quien* is only for people: for things and animals use *que*.
